variants.name: Broker-enforced per-message TTL (amqplib)
variants.implementation_notes: In Node the canonical realization is the transport's own TTL: channel.publish(exchange, key, content, { expiration: '60000' }) hands the broker a per-message TTL in milliseconds (a string on the wire; numbers are coerced) and a dead-letter exchange routes expired messages somewhere observable. This replaces any application timer: expiry survives restarts and multiple consumers, and a queue-level x-message-ttl covers a whole class of messages. Where there is no broker - in-process event buses, browser or worker queues - use the timer realization instead, because a JavaScript process cannot enforce anything it does not still hold.
pitfalls: RabbitMQ only evaluates per-message TTL when the message reaches the queue head, so a deep backlog keeps expired payloads in memory, and the effective policy can be capped by a queue-level TTL.
amqplib passes the option through unvalidated: undefined or NaN becomes no expiry at all, and publishing after the channel closed throws rather than reporting a problem.
Settling (ack/nack) decisions are independent of TTL - an expired message still occupies a delivery slot until it is settled or the consumer disconnects.

variants.name: Deadline field plus setTimeout / AbortSignal.timeout
variants.implementation_notes: Without a broker the deadline is data plus one timer: the producer stamps an absolute epoch-milliseconds expiresAt on the message and the consumer schedules removal with setTimeout (calling .unref() in Node so the timer does not keep the process alive) or aborts in-flight work with AbortSignal.timeout(ms), which rejects with a TimeoutError DOMException. This is the idiomatic replacement for a broker TTL inside one process, but it is per-process and best-effort: restarting the runtime forgets the timers and the event loop can fire them late, so every consumer still checks expiresAt on arrival. Keep broker TTL whenever messages outlive the process.
pitfalls: setTimeout is best-effort: under event-loop pressure it fires late, and in a browser a suspended tab or worker pauses it entirely; the expiresAt check must never be dropped.
Date.now() is a settable wall clock, so a clock step makes deadlines fire immediately or never - use performance.now() for local elapsed-time decisions and the absolute epoch only at the boundary.
Timers hold references: listeners on the signal or closures over large payloads keep them alive until the timeout settles, so remove listeners and unref timers to stay collectable.
